hook_clip: Here's how to reverse engineer CoSchedule from a written spec. Claude passed all twenty-seven checks, and found eight gaps in my spec.
outro_clip: The full spec is free at personal software factory dot com. If you build it, tell me what broke. I'm Sam. See you tomorrow.

scenes.text: We gave Claude one Markdown file. It copies the part of CoSchedule a small marketing team actually uses. One calendar for every channel, colored by channel. A record per piece, with an owner, a status and a publish date. An editor's approval before anything is scheduled. And campaigns you can move as a block.

The core rule is approval. Every piece moves through five steps. Idea, writing, in review, scheduled, published. The only way into scheduled is an editor's approval. And nobody approves their own piece. When Maya, an editor, sends her own post for review, it goes to Dana instead.

Claude built it in four phases, one prompt each. The foundation, with channels, campaigns and settings. Pieces, the calendar, the backlog and the pipeline. Review and publishing. Then reminders, overdue flags, the weekly digest and campaign moves. After every phase, the acceptance checks ran in a real browser, from fresh seed data.

Here's what it built. The month calendar puts each piece on its date in its channel color, and flags the overdue video. The pipeline board counts every status. A piece in review shows Approve and Request changes, with the full activity log. The weekly digest lists what publishes in the next seven days. And on a phone, the month becomes an agenda.
In the final browser run, all twenty-seven checks passed, along with sixty-three automated tests.

But the more useful result is what broke. The build exposed eight gaps in the spec. Places where Claude had to guess. Sign-in told strangers to ask an editor to add them, but no screen managed people. One part of the spec let editors withdraw any piece, while another said owner only. And a daily job at eight in the morning, team time, can't be one UTC cron schedule. Every gap is now fixed in the spec.

Passing every check isn't the same as production-ready. We didn't test production sign-in, sending email, the scheduled daily job, or several servers writing at once. Those are yours to check before a team relies on it.

So is it worth building? CoSchedule Starter is twenty-nine dollars a month, billed annually, for one user. Professional is forty-nine, with two users included. Campaigns are only on the Suite plan, from sixty-nine dollars a month. If you want posts published straight to social networks, with analytics, pay for CoSchedule. If your team just needs the plan, you mostly need the calendar, the approval step, and the reminders.
Everything is in one file. The data model, seventeen rules, seed data, four phase prompts, and all twenty-seven checks, with the eight fixes already in.
